abstract: This study examines the adoption and productivity effects of GitHub Copilot and Cursor using a proprietary dataset from Jellyfish covering approximately 200 million work events of 100,000 engineers at 500 firms. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, the authors find moderate productivity increases from AI adoption but no effects on output, task composition, or employment.
keyFindings: AI adoption led to an 8.5% increase in coding activity and 8.7% faster task completion with no measurable quality declines
These productivity gains did not translate into increased output, changes in task composition, or effects on employment
Even 18 months after firm-level adoption, only about half of engineers had begun using AI tools
Point estimates suggested marginally larger effects for senior workers, though differences were not statistically significant
Firms whose core product is software saw significant increases in output; firms using software as internal input saw no change
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting variation in timing of firm-level license purchases for GitHub Copilot and Cursor. Dataset: approximately 200 million work events of 100,000 engineers at 500 firms (Jellyfish data).
qualifiers: Productivity measures are based on coding activity metrics which may not capture full value of software development. The productivity-to-output gap suggests organizational factors mediate whether individual gains aggregate. Paper not yet widely available online.
